advisor.summary: The owner sells appreciating business interests to an intentionally defective grantor trust for an installment note at the applicable federal rate. Because Rev. Rul. 85-13 treats grantor and trust as one taxpayer, the sale triggers no gain and the note interest is neither income nor deduction — an income-tax non-event that freezes the estate at the note's value while all growth above the AFR accrues to the beneficiaries outside the transfer-tax base. The grantor's continued payment of the trust's income tax adds a further gift-tax-free wealth shift. Two facts discipline the recommendation post-OBBBA: the permanent $15 million exemption means many estates no longer need a freeze at all, and assets sold to the trust keep carryover basis, surrendering the step-up at death. This is an elevated-risk, counsel-led structure — the record is advisory, and the engine models none of it.
mechanics: The trust is drafted with a deliberate grantor-trust trigger — most commonly the §675(4)(C) power to substitute assets of equivalent value — leaving it defective for income tax under §§671-679 while staying outside the gross estate for transfer tax.

A seed gift, customarily about 10% of the intended purchase price, capitalizes the trust first so the note is respected as debt rather than a retained equity strip; a thin trust is the classic §2036 inclusion setup.

The sale closes at appraised fair market value against an installment note bearing at least the AFR (§1274(d); §7872 governs below-market recharacterization), commonly interest-only with a balloon. Under Rev. Rul. 85-13, no gain is recognized and no interest income or deduction arises while grantor status holds.

The freeze: the estate holds a note fixed at principal plus AFR interest, while every dollar of growth above that hurdle accrues in the trust for the beneficiaries — amplified where defensible minority or marketability discounts price the interests sold.

The tax burn: the grantor pays the income tax on all trust income, and Rev. Rul. 2004-64 confirms those payments are not additional gifts — the estate shrinks further while the trust compounds pre-tax.

The basis cost: trust assets keep carryover basis, and Rev. Rul. 2023-2 confirms no §1014 step-up at death for grantor-trust assets excluded from the gross estate. The substitution power lets the grantor swap high-basis assets in and pull low-basis assets back into the estate late in life, aiming the step-up where it matters.

authority.note: Grantor and grantor trust are one taxpayer — the sale is ignored for income tax, the hinge the entire structure turns on.
The grantor trust rules that render the trust defective for income tax purposes only.
The nonfiduciary substitution power — the customary defect trigger, doubling as the basis-management swap lever.
The grantor's payment of the trust's income tax is not a gift — the authority behind the tax-burn wealth shift.
The note must bear at least the AFR or the shortfall is recharacterized as a gift.
The inclusion risk: an undercapitalized trust, missed payments, or retained control pulls the transferred assets back into the gross estate at their date-of-death value.

authority.cite: Estate of Powell v. Commissioner, 148 T.C. 392 (2017)
authority.note: The Tax Court's expansive reading of §2036 retained control — the modern warning for transfers where the senior generation keeps its hands on the assets.
No basis step-up at death for grantor-trust assets outside the gross estate — the carryover-basis cost the freeze must outweigh.
The step-up the family forgoes on assets sold to the trust — quantify it against the estate tax saved before recommending.
The permanent $15M (indexed) basic exclusion — the threshold question of whether the client needs a freeze at all.

requirements: An estate realistically headed past the $15M-per-person (indexed) exemption, or high-growth assets on a credible path to exceed it.
A qualified appraisal of the interests sold, with any minority or marketability discounts defensibly supported.
A seed gift — roughly 10% of the purchase price is the practice norm, not a safe harbor — reported on Form 709 with adequate disclosure.
A real note: AFR or better, security, an enforced payment schedule, and trust cash flow (typically distributions from the interest sold) that can actually service it.
Estate counsel leads the drafting, with the CPA and appraiser coordinated — this is not a single-advisor project.
risks: §2036 inclusion is the leading audit theory: a thin seed gift, missed note payments, or retained control invites the government to pull the assets back into the estate at death-date value — Estate of Powell v. Commissioner, 148 T.C. 392 (2017) shows how far retained-control arguments now reach.
Valuation is the second front: discounts on closely held interests are the standing IRS attack, and only adequate-disclosure gift reporting starts the statute of limitations running.

The carryover-basis cost is real: for low-basis assets with modest growth, the income tax lost through the forfeited §1014 step-up (Rev. Rul. 2023-2) can exceed the estate tax saved — model both taxes before committing.
Death before the note is retired leaves genuinely unsettled income-tax questions on the unpaid balance; structure to retire the note during life where possible.

Ending grantor status mid-stream — deliberately or by drafting accident — can trigger gain to the extent the note balance exceeds basis, and the tax burn must stay affordable for as long as status holds.
Post-OBBBA, a freeze sized to the old sunset math may be unneeded complexity: below roughly $30M married, the permanent exemption often covers the estate without one.
stateNotes: States generally conform to the federal grantor-trust income-tax treatment through their federal starting points, but separate state estate and inheritance taxes with far lower exemptions can keep a freeze valuable even where the federal exemption covers the client — check every state of residence and property situs.

PTET interaction: pass-through interests sold to the trust can keep their entity-level PTET elections; while grantor status holds, the deemed-owner rules place the PTET deduction and any credit on the grantor's own returns.

Missouri imposes no state estate or inheritance tax and conforms to the federal income treatment through RSMo §143.121; the Missouri SALT Parity Act election (RSMo §143.436) keeps functioning for entity interests held by the trust.
reviewChecklist: Exemption math rerun under the permanent $15M (indexed) exclusion confirms the client genuinely needs a freeze.
Estate tax saved and §1014 step-up forgone are both modeled, and the net favors the transaction.
Seed gift meets or beats the customary 10% benchmark, and Form 709 with adequate disclosure is filed.
Note terms at AFR or better with security, a payment calendar in place, and the first payments actually made.
Appraisal quality and discount support reviewed by someone other than the appraiser.
A swap-power basis plan documented for late-life repositioning of low-basis assets.
Counsel, CPA, and appraiser roles coordinated in writing.

client.teaser: Lock the estate tax in at today's value — tomorrow's growth belongs to your family.
client.headline: Freeze your estate at today's value — the growth goes to your kids
plainEnglish: If your business is growing fast, the estate tax danger is not today's value. It is the value years from now. This plan freezes what the estate tax can ever see at today's number.

You set up a special family trust. Then you sell your business interest to it for a promissory note. Because of how the trust is built, the sale itself triggers no income tax. Your estate holds the note. The trust holds the business — and all its future growth — for your family.

There is a quiet extra push. You keep paying the income tax on what the trust earns. The IRS does not treat those payments as gifts. So your estate shrinks a little more each year while the trust grows untouched. One trade-off: the family keeps your old cost basis, so we weigh both taxes before you commit.
client.analogy: It is like selling the family orchard to your kids at today's price and taking back an IOU. Every harvest from now on is theirs. The taxman can only ever see the IOU.
benefits: The business's future growth happens outside your taxable estate
No income tax on the sale itself when structured correctly
Your ongoing tax payments quietly shift even more wealth to the family
Doubles as a real succession plan with the next generation in place
steps: WE model your estate with and without the freeze, cost-basis trade-off included.
WE coordinate the estate attorney who drafts the trust and the appraiser who prices the asset.
YOU make the seed gift and sign the sale papers; the note payments start on schedule.
WE check the plan every year — payments made, valuations current, the law unchanged.
clientCommitments: Keep the note real: payments on time, every time
Budget for the trust's income tax landing on your own return each year
Bring us and counsel in before any change to the trust or the business ownership

annualMaintenance: Annual note-payment compliance check with the trustee
Estate projection refresh as the exemption indexes and asset values move
Grantor-status confirmation and swap-power basis review
deliverables: Freeze feasibility memo — estate tax saved versus step-up forgone, both modeled
Transaction closing binder: trust, appraisal, note, security agreement, Form 709
Annual compliance letter documenting payments and valuations

suggest.reason: Selling to a grantor trust freezes estate value while income tax stays with the grantor.
